# Postpartum Cardiomyopathy(Archived)

**Authors:** Ateeq Mubarik, Venu Chippa, Karen Carlson, Arshad Muhammad Iqbal

**Source:** StatPearls - StatPearls Publishing

## Abstract

Peripartum cardiomyopathy (PPCM) is a rare form of congestive heart failure (CHF) of unknown etiology. Heart failure in the peripartum period was first described in 1849. In 2000, The National Heart Lung and Blood Institute and The Office of Rare Diseases workshop gave 4 criteria for PPCM, becoming the condition's first case definition. The 4 diagnostic criteria for PPCM are as follows: Cardiac failure in the last month of pregnancy or within 5 months of delivery. Absence of a determinable etiology for the cardiac failure. Absence of demonstrable structural cardiac disease before the last month of pregnancy. Echocardiographic evidence of diminished left ventricular systolic function noted by one of the following: Left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) below 45%, Motion-mode fractional shortening less than 30%. Left ventricular end-diastolic dimension exceeding 2.7 cm/m2. In the 2019 European Society of Cardiology position paper, Bauersachs and colleagues characterized PPCM based on 3 key criteria: heart failure due to left ventricular systolic dysfunction with an LVEF below 45%, onset near the end of pregnancy or during the postpartum period, and the absence of any other identifiable cause of heart failure. Notably, left ventricular dilation is not a required feature. An expanded definition of PPCM has been proposed to include 2 additional categories: early PPCM, which is diagnosed from the 1st to the 9th month of pregnancy, and late PPCM, which is identified between 6 and 12 months after delivery. This broader framework acknowledges variations in the timing of disease onset and extends beyond the traditional postpartum focus. PPCM is a diagnosis of exclusion. The incidence and prevalence of this condition vary widely, depending on race and geographic regions. The clinical outcome of PPCM is also diverse, ranging from complete recovery to death.
